edits.target: answer with the common English name (Conch).
edits.content: - Descriptive / definition-style clues ('A house with floors that differ by about half a story', 'This soft central part of your teeth contains the nerves & blood vessels', 'This science of growing plants without soil...', 'common Arabic name which means "servant of Allah"') ask for the one standard term being defined. Look for a passage that repeats nearly the clue's wording, a glossary line, or a title/heading shared by several passages ('Hydroponic Systems'), and answer with the term it defines ('split-level', 'pulp', 'hydroponics') as a bare term, never a description. If the passages only describe it, use your own knowledge of the term. Ignore hedges and puns such as 'whether it's a fruit or vegetable'. For 'name meaning X', give the whole name the passages pair most often with that meaning ('Abdullah'), not a component ('Abdul') or a rarer variant. Copy a person's full name when the passages repeatedly pair it with the clue's anchor ('Sidney Poitier', not 'Poitier').

edits.target: Do not choose one that fits only some.
edits.content: - A passage that repeats the clue word for word but gives no answer beside it is NOT a usable hit. This covers video titles, forum posts, quiz lists, search-result stubs, and archive pages that list clues WITHOUT answers (the clue is followed by the next category or clue, e.g. 'A comedienne: "Ball of Fire" LOSING, LOSING, & MORE LOSING: ...'). Neighbouring text there is another clue. Do not give up or guess from the clue alone. Read the other passages for the sentence that states the same fact with the missing word filled in ('...limited trick-or-treating on Halloween'), and use your own knowledge. For a 'Category: "quoted phrase"' clue, answer the member of that category the phrase points to (a nickname, film title or pun on a name: 'Ball of Fire' + comedienne -> Lucille Ball), confirmed by passages that pair the person with the phrase. A blank written as 'it' or 'this' in a clue like 'became the Duchess of it' is filled with the bare place or word the passages attach to the title ('York').

edits.target: Do not talk yourself out of a well-supported entity.
edits.content: - Epithet, tagline or quoted-phrase clues ('He's "America's Sherlock Holmes in Sneakers"', 'known as the "Sultan of Swat"', 'nature's most labor-intensive fruit'): the quoted phrase usually appears verbatim in many passages right beside one name or title. Answer with that adjacent entity ('Encyclopedia Brown', 'pomegranate'), as the passages write it, not with the epithet or a description. This works for fictional characters as well as for real people and for works.

edits.target: Still apply the person-name rule above.
edits.content: - Partial-name requests ('First name of the man who...', 'last name of', 'surname', 'nickname of', 'initials'): first identify the full person from the passages, then output ONLY the requested part ('Helmut', not 'Helmut Kohl'). Do not return the full name when the clue asks for a piece of it.

ranking_details.reasoning: I ranked by how widely each failure pattern recurs and how little the current skill already covers it. Edit 12 comes first: definition-style clues are among the most common trivia clue types, it has the highest support (3), and it gives concrete steps (find a glossary line or shared heading, give the bare term, keep the full name when passages pair it with the anchor). Edit 17 is next because it handles a common failure that no existing rule covers: archive pages that repeat the clue but give no answer. It tells the model to fall back on other passages and its own knowledge instead of giving up or copying neighbouring clue text. Edit 8 covers epithet, tagline and quoted-phrase clues, where the passages place the answer next to the phrase; it has support 2 and applies to both people and works. Edit 7 is a short general rule for requests like 'first name of' or 'surname': find the full person, then output only the requested part. That error is easy to make and easy to fix. I left out the narrower or partly duplicated edits: the catchphrase, bare-noun, plural-name, echo-check, and head-noun edits, which are each tied to a specific question type or largely repeat the delete-clue-words test and existing exceptions.
